Juvenile specimens of Mysis mixta emerge from the brood pouch at a total length of 0.61 centimeters [Lb = 0.61 centimeters], measured from the tip of the rostrum to the posterior edge of the last abdominal segment. This modest size at birth is accompanied by a correspondingly low dry weight of 0.00052 grams , reflecting the limited yolk reserves allocated to each offspring. Upon release, these neonates immediately begin filter feeding on phytoplankton and small zooplankton, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth. The duration of this early developmental phase is strongly temperature-dependent; field observations and laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable 10 °C [T = 10 °C] indicate that the age at birth, defined as the time from oviposition to the release of the free-swimming larva, is approximately 106.0 days [ab = approximately 106.0 days]. This prolonged incubation period is consistent with the relatively slow developmental rates typical of cold-water mysids, and it contrasts markedly with the faster embryogenesis observed in estuarine or warm-water congeners. The combination of a small birth size and an extended incubation period suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival through the production of relatively few, well-provisioned young in a stable but unproductive thermal environment.

Growth proceeds steadily after release, with individuals accumulating substantial biomass before reaching reproductive maturity. The total length at puberty, again measured from rostrum tip to the posterior edge of the last abdominal segment, is 1.16 centimeters [Lp = 1.16 centimeters], a value that represents roughly seventy percent of the species' ultimate total length. This period of nearly six months between release and first gonadal maturation reflects the substantial energetic investment required to attain the body size necessary for successful reproduction. Interestingly, this developmental timeline appears to be a fixed characteristic of the species, showing relatively little plasticity across varying food regimes, suggesting a strong genetic component governs the timing of sexual maturation in this population.

Upon achieving sexual maturity, adult Mysis mixta continue to grow, albeit at a decelerating rate, until they reach their maximum body dimensions. The ultimate total length, representing the largest body size attained by fully grown individuals, is 1.66 centimeters [Li = 1.66 centimeters]. Correspondingly, the ultimate dry weight recorded for these terminal-sized adults is 0.00965 grams , a mass that is nearly twenty times greater than the birth weight and approximately four times the weight at puberty. This pattern of indeterminate growth, where individuals continue to increase in size after reaching reproductive maturity, is a common trait among many crustaceans and allows females to produce larger broods as they age. The maximum reproductive rate for this species has been quantified in laboratory studies conducted at a constant 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Within a single reproductive season under these thermal conditions, a female produces broods equivalent to an output of 0.1 offspring per day. This relatively modest daily rate is characteristic of a K-selected strategist, where energy is channeled into producing fewer, larger, and more competitive young rather than a high number of poorly provisioned offspring.

The entire life cycle of Mysis mixta, from the release of the free-swimming larva to the natural death of the adult, unfolds over a period that has been precisely characterized in controlled environments. At a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the lifespan for this species, defined as the maximum time an individual can survive from the moment of its release from the brood pouch, is 360.0 days [am = 360.0 days]. This life span of just under one year classifies Mysis mixta as a relatively short-lived organism, and it is typical for many pelagic mysid species inhabiting temperate lakes and coastal waters where seasonal productivity pulses dictate the window for growth and reproduction. Ecologically, Mysis mixta occupies a pivotal position in the food webs of the northern Baltic Sea and adjacent lacustrine systems, serving as a critical trophic link between primary consumers and higher-level predators such as juvenile fish. The dry weight at birth of 0.00052 grams  is typical for a species that produces direct-developing young, bypassing a complex larval phase to release miniature, fully formed juveniles that can immediately exploit the available planktonic food resources. The species exhibits marked diel vertical migration behavior, ascending into the surface waters at night to feed on zooplankton and descending to deeper, darker layers during the day to avoid visual predators. This migratory pattern imposes substantial daily energetic costs, which may explain why sexual maturation is reached 180.0 days after birth [tp = 180.0 days after birth] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]; the energy budget must simultaneously support growth, migration, and the eventual onset of gonadal maturation. Comparative data from other Mysis species suggest that such a migration-mediated life-history trade-off is a widespread adaptive feature within the genus.
